title: The Goat, the Stoat, and the Lighthouse Prize
markdown:
Once upon a time, at the Market of Many Wonders, banners snapped and the air smelled of roasted nuts, for it was the day of the Coastal Caretaker competition.

Luca, a fluffy white goat in a stiff apron, felt more costume than competitor. “Wise old lighthouse keeper,” he muttered, practising a nod that twitched. “Not a goat craving clover.”

Beside him Hazel the stoat worked with quiet focus, plaster-dusted, coiling tiny rope around a miniature lighthouse. She believed in action. She had made the lamp gleam, updated the keeper’s log with a grumpy seagull, organised spare flares like a professional.

Inspector Sterling, dapper puffin, waddled over, sharp eyes on the displays. “Luca, I presume?”

“Indeed! Luca, at your service. And this,” a gesture—Hazel’s polite nod—“is my very capable partner.”

Trial one: Sterling lifted a spare wick. “Preferred preparation? Crucial factors?”

Luca launched into fibre and paraffin, conveniently forgetting Hazel had found better wicks because the old ones smoked. “A decent wick wants honesty,” the little lamp seemed to say, or so Luca heard in the brass, and he talked louder to cover it.

Trial two: the model’s base wobbled as Sterling examined it. “Oh dear,” Luca whispered. Hazel slid a wooden wedge under, stopping the tremor. Sterling, however, saw Luca fumbling the lamp. “Contingency for severe storms?”

“We secure everything. Thoroughly. And we… hum cheerful shanties.”

Hazel checked a miniature rain gauge. She had already reinforced shutters Luca had called unnecessary fussing while he polished brass.

The pattern held. Luca presented grandeur; a hiccup appeared—a wobbly tripod, a loose wire. Hazel fixed it. Wind threatened spare bulbs; her paw steadied them. Luca’s polish left a smudge; she buffed it. Sterling watched the strained performance and missed the competence.

Trial three, the hardest: emergency lighting. Luca flipped a switch. Nothing. Harder. Darkness. His nose twitched.

“A minor technical difficulty, Mr Luca?”

The facade crumbled. “I do not understand. I checked everything!”

Hazel, patient sigh spent, stood. “The wires are loose near the battery. They need reseating.” Nimble paws, insulating tape, a flip. LEDs woke.

Sterling blinked, a faint smile. “Remarkable. And this exceptionally capable individual?”

Luca looked at her, embarrassment and admiration mixed. “That is Hazel. My partner. She has been keeping everything running. I was mostly trying to look in charge.”

“You understand practical application, young stoat. Your subtle interventions have not gone unnoticed.”

Later, paper lanterns lifting, Luca nudged her. “I am sorry. I was so busy looking the expert I forgot what matters. You are the real caretaker.”

“We are a team,” Hazel said, eyes softening. “Sometimes the best help is doing what needs doing.” She freed a lantern string from a fruit stall.

Sterling awarded the prize to both, praising exceptional partnership. Luca beamed, genuine, and made sure she stood beside him. Being expert was the work, not the apron. Honesty, he found, was funnier than any rehearsed nod.

And so the goat learned to share the lamp, and their tale is still told when lanterns rise over the market.

Thus a prize for looking in charge is a poor light; the one who reseats the wire is the keeper.
